notes.short: The conqueror as a fisherman hauling in nations
notes.about: The prophet pictures the Chaldean conqueror as a fisherman. Men are like fish with no ruler; he hauls them up with hook and nets, then sacrifices to his net, as if his gear had won the catch. The last verse gives the meaning: will he go on slaying nations without mercy?

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: The foe pulls all of them up with a hook
figure.means: the Chaldean sweeping nations into captivity; his hook and nets stand for every means by which he subdues and destroys them

notes.evidence: Adam Clarke says the last verse explains the allegory of the net; as fishermen cast again and again, Nebuchadnezzar destroys nation after nation. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the prophet likens men to fish, Nebuchadnezzar to a fisherman. C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says it is told in figures from a fisherman's life, hook and nets being all the Chaldeans' means of conquest.
notes.limit: One writer notes that the picture gives way to plain speech in the last clause of the last verse.

cites.quote: Like the fishermen, who throw cast after cast while any fish are to be caught, so Nebuchadnezzar is destroying one nation after another. This last sentence explains the allegory of the net.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: All may fish in the sea with impunity; so the Chaldeans with impunity afflict Thy people, as these have no longer the God of the theocracy, their King, to defend them. ... He compares the world to the sea; men to fishes; Nebuchadnezzar to a fisherman ( Hab 1:15-17 ).
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This strange fact is depicted still further in Hab 1:14-16 in figures taken from the life of a fisherman. The men are like fishes, whom the Chaldaean collects together in his net ... the hook, the net, and the fishing net ... refer to all the means which the Chaldaeans employ in order to subdue and destroy the nations. ... In the last clause the figure passes over into a literal address.

notes.short: Stones and rafters cry out against the builder
notes.about: The stones of the wall cry out and the rafters echo them, as if the house could speak. The picture shows that every part of a house built by unjust gain (verse 9) bears witness against the man who built it. Some add that it cries out to God for vengeance.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: the stones will cry out from the wall, and the rafters will echo it from the woodwork
figure.means: the house built by plunder and cruelty bearing witness against its builder and, some add, crying to God for vengeance

notes.evidence: Calvin calls it a new personification: the prophet gives speech to stone and wood, and every part of the building cries that it was built by plunder. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) also calls it personification: the stones testify against the plunderer. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes): such works have a voice that cries to God. Clarke: stone and timber are represented as calling for vengeance.

cites.quote: There is here introduced by the Prophet a new personification. … He now ascribes speech to stones and wood, of which buildings are formed. … there is no part of the building that will not cry out that it was built by plunder, by cruelty, and, in a word, by evil deeds.
personification. The very stones of thy palace built by rapine shall testify against thee

cites.quote: great works, performed amid wrong and cruelty and for man's ambition and pride, have a voice too, and cry out to God, calling down His vengeance on the oppressor. … Did not the blood and groans of men cry out to God, speechless things have a voice to appeal to Him

cites.quote: therefore the stones and the timber are represented as calling out for vengeance against this ruthless conqueror.

notes.short: A saying the plundered nations will take up
notes.about: The nations the conqueror gathered to himself (verse 5) will turn his deeds into a saying against him: “Woe to him who amasses what is not his.” Short and pointed, it would be repeated everywhere when the plunderer fell.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: Woe to him who amasses what is not his
figure.means: the saying the wronged nations will repeat against the plunderer: wealth taken from others brings him woe, not gain

original.note: In Hebrew “taunt” is mashal, a word for a short, pointed saying.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia, among proverbs first found in Scripture. Calvin says this woe would be said everywhere, the mashal being a short, pithy saying worth remembering. Henry says those triumphing in the tyrant's fall are given a taunting proverb, the woe its words. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) has the nations sing a dirge of woes: proverbs saying much in few words.
notes.limit: The verse foretells a saying the nations will take up when he falls; it does not say the words were already in use. It is the first of five woes in the chapter (verses 6, 9, 12, 15 and 19).

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 763
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture; but, which, owing to their fulness of meaning and their wide application, have since passed into general use as proverbial sayings ... “Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say, ‘Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his!
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: all these would at length take up against them parables and taunts; and what would be said everywhere would be this ... Woe to him who increases and enriches himself by things not his own. ... meshil is a short saying or a pithy sentence, and worthy to be remembered

Those that shall triumph in the fall of this great tyrant are here furnished with a parable, and a taunting proverb, to take up against him. He shall say (he that draws up the insulting ditty shall say thus), Ho, he that increases that which is not his!

As one vast choir in one terrible varied chant of all those thousand thousand voices, to sing a dirge over him of the judgments of God which his ill-doings to them should bring upon him, a fivefold Woe, woe, woe, woe, woe! ... It is the character of these proverbs to say much in few words, sometimes in one, and more than appears.

notes.short: Making the neighbors drunk to see their shame
notes.about: In the fourth woe the conqueror is pictured as a host who makes his neighbors drunk to gaze at their shame. It pictures his luring nearby nations into his own greed for conquest, only to bring them down. Then the cup turns, and he must drink from the LORD's right hand and be covered with disgrace.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: Woe to him who gives drink to his neighbors
figure.means: the Chaldean drawing the nations around him into his own greed for war and plunder, and so bringing them to ruin and shame

notes.evidence: John Calvin calls the passage allegorical, likening the king's endless greed to drunkenness. C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it an allegory of making nations drink the cup of wrath, pointing to the artifices by which he subdues them. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a metaphor: the king lured nearby states into his thirst for war and booty, then shamed them.

cites.quote: I therefore doubt not but that this whole discourse, in which the Babylonian king is condemned for making drunk his associates or friends, is metaphorical or allegorical. ... He indeed compares the insatiable avarice of that king to intemperance ... Since, then, he had thus blinded many kings, they are said to have been inebriated by him.

The description in Hab 2:15 and Hab 2:16 is figurative ... The prostrate condition of the drunken man is a figurative representation of the overthrow of a conquered nation ... This allegory, in which the conquest and subjugation of the nations are represented as making them drink of the cup of wrath ... points to the artifices with which he overpowers them
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: English Version keeps up the metaphor better. It is not enough for thee to be "drunken" thyself, unless thou canst lead others into the same state. The thing meant is, that the Chaldean king, with his insatiable desires (a kind of intoxication), allured neighboring states into the same mad thirst for war to obtain booty, and then at last exposed them to loss and shame
